notes: Replaced associative-subscript-string with associative-empty-key-rejection to avoid mirroring indexed-arithmetic-subscript.

cards.statement: With declare -a a=(red blue), Bash puts red at index zero.
cards.explanation: Implicit indices in an indexed compound assignment start at zero, so red occupies a[0].

cards.statement: With declare -A a, Bash accepts a['']=ready as an entry whose key is an empty string.
cards.explanation: Associative array keys are nonempty strings, so this assignment fails instead of creating an empty-key entry.
cards.misconception: An associative array accepts an empty string as a key.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([2]=x [9]=y), Bash makes ${#a[@]} report the highest index plus one.
cards.explanation: The expansion counts assigned elements, so this sparse array reports 2.
cards.misconception: An indexed array's element count includes its index gaps.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([3]=yes), Bash expands ${a[1+2]} to the value yes.
cards.explanation: Bash evaluates the indexed subscript as an arithmetic expression, selecting index 3.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([2]=x [9]=y), Bash expands ${a[-8]} to the value stored at index 2.
cards.explanation: Negative indexed subscripts count back from one greater than the maximum index, including gaps.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([4]=x y), Bash places the unindexed value y at index zero.
cards.explanation: Within this compound assignment, the omitted subscript follows the last assigned index, placing y at index 5.
cards.misconception: An omitted subscript restarts implicit indexing after an explicit index.

cards.statement: For indexed a=(x y), Bash keeps the existing elements when it executes a+=(z).
cards.explanation: The += compound assignment appends the new member while retaining the previous members.

cards.statement: For indexed a=('red blue' ''), Bash supplies two arguments through "${a[@]}".
cards.explanation: Quoted "${a[@]}" supplies one argument per element, retaining the embedded space and the empty element.

cards.statement: For associative a=([red]=x), Bash expands ${!a[@]} to the stored value x.
cards.explanation: The ${!a[@]} expansion supplies assigned keys, so this array yields red.
cards.misconception: The array key expansion returns element values.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([2]=red [5]=blue [9]=green), Bash expands "${a[@]:2:2}" to red and blue arguments.
cards.explanation: The offset starts at numeric index 2; the length selects two assigned elements despite the gaps.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Arrays and Parameter Expansion

cards.statement: For indexed a=(x y), Bash shifts y to index zero after unset 'a[0]'.
cards.explanation: Unsetting an indexed element leaves surviving indices in place, so y remains at index 1.
cards.misconception: Removing an indexed element compacts the remaining indices.

cards.statement: For indexed a=([3]=x), Bash expands the unsubscripted "$a" to the value x.
cards.explanation: An unsubscripted array reference selects element 0. Since that element is unset here, "$a" yields an empty string.
cards.misconception: A bare array reference selects its first populated element.

cards.statement: Bash selects the then branch when an if condition returns status zero.
cards.explanation: An if command uses the condition's exit status to select its branch; zero selects the then list.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: When an if condition succeeds, Bash still evaluates the subsequent elif conditions.
cards.explanation: A successful condition selects its branch and ends the selection process, so subsequent elif conditions are skipped.
cards.misconception: Bash evaluates later elif conditions after choosing an earlier branch.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: With value='a b', Bash treats $value as one operand in [[ $value == 'a b' ]].
cards.explanation: Inside [[ ]], parameter expansions skip word splitting, leaving the embedded space inside the operand.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: Bash gives [ -n ] a failure status because the string operand is absent.
cards.explanation: The [ builtin sees the nonempty string -n as its single expression argument, so the test succeeds.
cards.misconception: A lone -n inside [ ] is interpreted as an incomplete unary test.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: test and [ Builtins

cards.statement: With LC_ALL=C, Bash evaluates [[ 20 < 3 ]] as a successful string comparison.
cards.explanation: The < operator compares strings lexically; the leading character 2 sorts before 3 in the C locale.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

cards.statement: Bash compares the text 2+2 and 4 literally in [[ 2+2 -eq 4 ]].
cards.explanation: Inside [[ ]], -eq evaluates its operands as arithmetic expressions, so 2+2 compares equal to 4.
cards.misconception: The integer comparison primary compares operand text instead of evaluating expressions.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

cards.statement: With value='', Bash evaluates [[ -v value ]] as a successful variable test.
cards.explanation: The -v primary checks whether the variable has an assigned value; an empty assigned value qualifies.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

cards.statement: Given an empty regular file f, Bash evaluates [[ -s f ]] as a successful file test.
cards.explanation: The -s primary tests for a file whose size exceeds zero, so an empty regular file fails it.
cards.misconception: The -s primary succeeds merely because a regular file exists.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Expressions

cards.statement: Bash treats the right operand in [[ abc == a* ]] as a shell pattern.
cards.explanation: The unquoted pattern a* matches abc, so this conditional expression succeeds.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: With re='a.*', Bash matches abc in the expression [[ abc =~ "$re" ]].
cards.explanation: Quoting "$re" makes the regex operand literal, so abc fails to match the literal text a.*.
cards.misconception: A quoted regex variable retains its regular-expression operators.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: After [[ abc123 =~ ([a-z]+)([0-9]+) ]], Bash sets BASH_REMATCH[0] to abc.
cards.explanation: BASH_REMATCH[0] holds the whole matched substring, abc123. The first parenthesized group belongs to index 1.
cards.misconception: BASH_REMATCH starts its captured parenthesized groups at index zero.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: With x=0, Bash leaves x at zero after [[ yes == yes || ++x -eq 1 ]].
cards.explanation: The left comparison succeeds, so || skips the right expression and its increment.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Conditional Constructs

cards.statement: Bash re-expands a for loop's in words between successive iterations.
cards.explanation: Bash expands the item list before iteration begins; body changes leave that prepared list intact.
cards.misconception: A for loop regenerates its item list during iteration.

cards.statement: Bash uses positional parameters as the items in for item; do :; done.
cards.explanation: Omitting the in clause selects the positional parameters as the loop's iteration items.

cards.statement: With item=old, Bash leaves item=new after for item in; do item=new; done.
cards.explanation: An empty item list skips the body and makes no assignment to the loop variable, leaving item equal to old.
cards.misconception: An empty for item list produces one iteration with an empty value.

cards.statement: Bash runs i=0 once when it enters the arithmetic loop for ((i=0; i<3; i++)).
cards.explanation: The initialization runs before the repeating condition, body and step sequence.

cards.statement: Bash enters the body in while false; true; do break; done because its final test succeeds.
cards.explanation: The while condition uses its list's final command status; true supplies zero and admits the body.

cards.statement: Bash runs the body of until true; do :; done before evaluating its initial condition.
cards.explanation: An until loop checks its condition first, so the initial successful true skips this body.
cards.misconception: An until loop performs a body iteration before its first condition check.

cards.statement: Inside two nested Bash loops, break 2 resumes execution after the outer loop.
cards.explanation: The numeric argument selects how many enclosing loops break terminates.

cards.statement: Inside two nested arithmetic for loops, Bash makes continue 2 run the outer loop's step expression.
cards.explanation: The second enclosing loop resumes at its step expression, followed by its next condition check.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: continue and Arithmetic Loops

cards.statement: With ;; clause terminators, Bash executes the last matching clause in a case command.
cards.explanation: Bash examines clauses in source order; the first matching clause ending in ;; completes dispatch.
cards.misconception: case selects the final matching clause when patterns overlap.

cards.statement: In a Bash case clause, red|blue) selects the same body when either pattern matches.
cards.explanation: The | separator groups alternative patterns for a single case clause.

cards.statement: After a matching case clause, Bash's ;;& runs the next body before testing the next clause's pattern.
cards.explanation: The ;;& terminator resumes pattern testing. The ;& terminator instead proceeds directly to the next body.
cards.misconception: The ;;& terminator falls through directly to the next clause's commands.

cards.statement: Bash treats the pattern "a"* in a case clause as the literal text a*.
cards.explanation: Quoting part of a case pattern makes that part literal; the unquoted * stays active, so "a"* matches abc.
cards.misconception: Quoting one part of a case pattern makes the entire pattern literal.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: case and Pattern Matching

cards.statement: After f changes its arguments with set -- and returns, Bash restores the caller's positional parameters.
cards.explanation: The caller's positional parameters are saved for the function call and restored when it finishes.

cards.statement: When f calls itself, Bash makes the inner local x declaration reuse the outer call's local x.
cards.explanation: A recursive invocation gets its own local x. The outer invocation's local variable stays separate.
cards.misconception: Recursive calls share a single instance of a declared local variable.

cards.statement: During a function call, Bash changes $0 to the name of the function being executed.
cards.explanation: A function call leaves $0 holding the shell or script identity.
cards.misconception: The function name replaces the shell or script identity in $0.

cards.statement: Inside f, return 7 gives the function call an exit status of 7.
cards.explanation: A numeric argument to return supplies the function's status to its caller.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and return

cards.statement: Inside a function, Bash handles exit 7 by ending the call and resuming its caller.
cards.explanation: exit terminates the shell executing the function.
cards.misconception: exit inside a function ends the function call while keeping its caller running.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and exit

cards.statement: For f(){ true; false; }, Bash reports a failure status when f reaches the end of its body.
cards.explanation: A function reaching its closing brace returns its last executed command's status, here the failure from false.

cards.statement: With global x=old, f(){ declare x=new; }; f changes the global x to new.
cards.explanation: Inside a function, plain declare creates a variable local to that call; declare -g selects global scope.
cards.misconception: A plain declare inside a function updates a same-named global variable.

cards.statement: For g(){ printf %s "$x"; } and f(){ local x=inner; g; }, Bash prints inner when f runs.
cards.explanation: Bash's dynamic scope makes a caller's local x visible to the helper it invokes.

cards.statement: With global x=outer, f(){ local x=inner; x=changed; }; f leaves the global x equal to outer.
cards.explanation: Assignments target f's local x. After f returns, the earlier global binding is visible again.

cards.statement: Bash applies a positive FUNCNEST limit separately to the recursion depth of individual functions.
cards.explanation: FUNCNEST limits the total depth of active function calls, including chains through different functions.
cards.misconception: FUNCNEST assigns a separate recursion allowance to each function.

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Functions and FUNCNEST

cards.statement: With indexed a=([2]=old) and $1=a inside f, Bash's scalar local -n ref=$1 makes ref[2]=x change a[2].
cards.explanation: The local scalar nameref points to the array named by the argument, so assignment through ref[2] reaches a[2].

source.title: GNU Bash man page: Parameters and Namerefs

cards.statement: With nullglob off, f(){ local -; shopt -s nullglob; }; f restores nullglob to off.
cards.explanation: local - restores options changed through set. This shopt change persists, so nullglob remains enabled.
cards.misconception: local - restores shopt settings together with set options.
